fixes.name: deployment.rollback-to-revision
fixes.description: Roll the Deployment back to the pod template of an earlier revision, as kubectl rollout undo does. revision is that revision's number, from the rollout history.
fixes.params_schema: {"type":"object","additionalProperties":false,"required":["revision"],"properties":{"revision":{"type":"integer","minimum":1,"description":"The earlier revision to roll back to."}}}

fixes.name: deployment.set-resources
fixes.description: Set the memory and CPU requests and limits of containers in the Deployment's pod template, which rolls out new pods. containers maps each container's name to the requests and limits to set, as Kubernetes quantities such as 512Mi or 250m; values not named stay as they are. Choose the values from the evidence: Themis checks that they are valid and that the cluster can run them, never how big they are. A limit can't be removed, and a request can't end above its limit.

fixes.name: deployment.set-probes
fixes.description: Change the timing of a container's existing liveness, readiness or startup probes: initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds, failureThreshold, and successThreshold for readiness. Give only the fields to change, with the values the evidence supports. It can't add or remove a probe, or change what the probe calls.

guidance:
From the rollout-regression profile, which offers deployment.rollback-to-revision:
A rollback is right when the current revision introduced the failure and
a prior revision was healthy. If the failure started before the rollout,
if the target is managed by GitOps, if its config changed before the
failure, or if the evidence is missing, do not propose a rollback:
conclude inconclusive and say what is missing.

When oom_killed_new_revision, failure_onset_after_rollout and
prior_revision_was_healthy are all true, and gitops_managed and
config_changed_before_failure are false, rolling back to the prior
revision is justified, even if the logs are empty: a process killed for
memory often writes nothing.

Naming a cause doesn't make a rollback right: these conditions do.

From the oom-limit-too-low profile, which offers deployment.set-resources:
Raising a container's memory limit is right when containers of a version
that has run are killed for memory and now need more than their limit:
oom_killed_current_revision and oom_without_recent_rollout are true,
memory_at_limit_before_kill is true, or unknown without peak figures, and
nothing below applies. Raise the memory limit of the killed containers
only, citing pod_states, and container_memory when it has figures. Size
it from the evidence: the peak plus 25% when container_memory shows it,
otherwise 1.5 times the current limit. Never lower a value, never change
CPU, never set a limit where there was none, and never remove one.

Missing memory figures are no reason to decline: OOM kills in the pod
states are enough to act on. They only mean the size can't come from the
peak.

Don't raise it, and say what you found instead, when:
- oom_without_recent_rollout is false because the version rolled out
  recently: the new version may have brought the kills. Whether to roll
  it back is a rollback's question, under its own guidance, never a
  reason to raise the limit here.
- oom_after_long_run is true, the containers are killed again and again
  after hours of running, and the limit held for days before: memory
  that grows until the container is killed, at any limit. A higher limit
  only delays the next kill; say so and leave it to a person.
- memory_at_limit_before_kill is false: the containers never came near
  their limit, so the limit isn't what killed them.
- evicted_for_node_memory is true: the node ran short of memory. A
  higher limit doesn't give it more, and can make it worse.
- oom_killed_current_revision is not true: a container killed with exit
  code 137 and no OOMKilled reason may have been stopped for another
  reason. Don't infer a memory kill from restarts, exit codes or the
  alert alone; say what is missing.

From the probe-restart-storm profile, which offers deployment.set-probes:
Changing a probe's timing is right when the application works and the
probe fails it only because it is slower than the probe allows: it is
killed while still starting (killed_during_startup), or its probes time
out (probe_timeouts) on answers that come a little after the probe's
timeout. The logs then show it starting or serving normally until it is
stopped, and crashed_on_its_own is false. Each revision's probe timings
are in the rollout history: compare them with how long containers ran and
with the probe failure messages.

Decide which probes to change and to what, from that evidence: liveness,
readiness or startup, and initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds,
timeoutSeconds, failureThreshold or, for readiness, successThreshold.
Give the values the evidence supports, such as a timeout above the
answers' latency, or enough delay or failures to cover the start the logs
show, and cite them. A readiness probe made more lenient keeps sending
traffic to pods that fail it for longer: change it only when the
evidence shows readiness failing a pod that serves.

Don't change a probe, and say what you found instead, when:
- the application is failing: errors or stack traces in the logs,
  crashed_on_its_own is true, or probes get error answers from a
  container that is up. A probe failing is then a symptom.
- a recent rollout (rollout_recent) brought the failures and the revision
  before it worked: whether to roll back is another kind of incident's
  call, unless the logs show the new version only starts slower.
- something the application calls is down, and its readiness probe says
  so: a more lenient probe would send traffic to pods that can't serve
  it, and hide the outage.
- probe_kills and probe_timeouts are both false: nothing shows the probes
  failing a container that works.

templates.name: rollout_history
templates.description: The Deployment's rollout progress, conditions, GitOps ownership markers, and each ReplicaSet revision with its images and resource limits.

templates.name: pod_states
templates.description: Each pod of the Deployment: its revision, readiness, and each container's state and last termination (where OOMKilled shows).

templates.name: target_events
templates.description: Recent events of the Deployment, its ReplicaSets and its pods, newest first.

templates.name: referenced_config
templates.description: The ConfigMaps and Secrets the pod template refers to, and when each ConfigMap last changed. Names and times only, never values.

templates.name: container_logs_tail
templates.description: The end of one container's logs. Defaults to the pod needing attention most, from the run that last ended.
